facts.statement: The genus Lunaspis was first described by Broili in 1929.
The species Lunaspis heroldi was discovered by Ferdinand Broili in Germany in 1929.
facts.quote: Broili discovered L. heroldi in 1929 in Germany.

facts.statement: The species Lunaspis broilii is commonly larger than Lunaspis heroldi.
facts.quote: L. Broilii is very commonly larger than L. heroldi.

facts.statement: Lunaspis lived in shallow marine environments during the Early Devonian, between approximately 409.1 and 402.5 million years ago.
facts.quote: Lunaspis is an extinct genus of armor-plated petalichthyid placoderm fish that lived in shallow marine environments of the Early Devonian period, from approximately 409.1 to 402.5 million year ago.

facts.statement: Fossils of Lunaspis have been found in Germany, China, and Australia.
facts.quote: Fossils have been found in Germany, China and Australia.

facts.statement: Lunaspis were flat fish with elongated pectoral spines, shortened thoracic armor, and eyes oriented dorsally.
facts.quote: Like many other petalichthyid fish, Lunaspis are flat and have elongated pectoral spines, shortened thoracic armor, and dorsally oriented eyes.

facts.statement: Lunaspis had long, thin tails that resembled whips, similar to modern skates and rays.
facts.quote: The tails are long and thin and resemble a whip, somewhat like extant skates and rays.

facts.statement: The long, spine-like plates of Lunaspis suggest a crescent moon shape, which inspired the genus name 'moon-shield'.
facts.quote: These long, spine-like plates give the suggestion of a crescent moon, hence the generic name (moon-shield).

facts.statement: Lunaspis were marine bottom-dwelling nektonic carnivores.
facts.quote: Lunaspis were marine bottom dwelling creatures, like many other Devonian placoderm fish, and were nektonic carnivores.

facts.statement: The body of Lunaspis was compressed dorsoventrally, similar to other petalichthyid fish.
facts.quote: The body shape of Lunaspis is also similar to other petalichthyid fish, compressed dorsoventrally.

facts.statement: Specimens of L. broilii and L. heroldi from Australia show tubercles on the median dorsal plate that coalesce into a distinct median dorsal ridge.
facts.quote: According to specimens examined from the Taemas-Wee Jasper region of New South Wales in Australia, both L. broilii and L. herolfi have tubercles of the median dorsal plate coalesce into a distinct median dorsal ridge (MDR).

facts.statement: The fusion of tubercles into a ridge is unique to Lunaspis within the order Petalichthyida.
facts.quote: The fusion of the tubercles is unique to Lunaspis in the order Petalichthyida, where other devonian fish in this order have ornament tubercles that are separately occurring.

facts.statement: The curved spinal plates of Lunaspis acted as wings off the center armor and featured many small spines along their anterior ridge.
facts.quote: The spinal plates are curved and are the wings off of the center part of the bony armoring. They have many small spines along the anterior ridge of spinal plates.

facts.statement: Lunaspis was originally classified in the family Acanthaspidae, but Walter Gross's 1937 findings led to its reclassification into the family Macropetalichthyidae after Acanthaspis was synonymized with it.
facts.quote: Lunaspis was originally placed within the family Acanthaspidae, but according to Walter Gross's findings in 1937, the type genus of Acanthaspidae, Acanthaspis, was synonymized with Lunaspis, and the entire family merged into the family Macropetalichthyidae.

facts.statement: Lunaspis belongs to the family Macropetalichthyidae.
Lunaspis belongs to the order Petalichthyida.
Lunaspis is classified as a placoderm.
The time range for Lunaspis is the Emsian stage, from 410.62 to 399.5 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Emsian to Emsian (410.62 to 399.5 million years ago)
